text:
When I joined Marlow Vale Borough Council as a finance officer, the monthly budget reports for our waste and recycling service routinely arrived two weeks late and nobody trusted them. Managers kept their own spreadsheets, and the figures never agreed. I decided to find out why.

I began by pulling invoice and fleet-cost extracts from the finance system with SQL, joining them to the depot's vehicle and rota tables. Within a week I found that about 6% of invoices were coded to the wrong cost centre, and that two depots defined "agency spend" differently. I wrote a short data dictionary covering every field and its source, and agreed a single definition with both depot managers. I also removed driver names and payroll numbers from the extracts before sharing them, keeping only role codes, because most readers did not need personal details. Then I built a repeatable SQL script and an Excel workbook that flagged mismatched codes and missing entries before each month-end.

The harder part was explaining the results. The depot supervisors did not care about cost centres; they cared about overtime. I sat with them on a Tuesday morning and showed one chart: overtime hours per collection round, month by month. It revealed that two rounds were generating nearly a third of overtime because of a badly timed tip schedule. For the finance committee, I wrote a one-page summary with a single recommendation and the likely saving, about £38,000 a year.

I did this alongside the depot managers, who corrected my assumptions twice, and I shared the scripts with a colleague so the process did not depend on me. Reports now go out within four working days, and the supervisors adjusted the two rounds in the spring. I would like to bring the same approach to Example Co.'s sales, inventory and delivery data.

In my two years as a research assistant at the Hallowmere Institute for Social Research, the project that taught me the most was a study of how commuting costs affected school attendance across 40 neighbourhoods. The data arrived as nine survey exports, a transport fare table and attendance records from a regional education office, and none of them shared a clean key. I wrote SQL in PostgreSQL to join them, using household postcodes mapped to neighbourhood codes, and built aggregation queries that produced attendance rates by term, fare band and distance. Along the way I used Python with pandas for the reshaping that was awkward in SQL, and I produced the final summary tables in Excel.

The joins exposed problems. About 6 percent of survey rows had duplicate household IDs, and the attendance file recorded absences in two different ways after a system change in the second term. I wrote a set of checks that counted duplicates, flagged impossible dates and compared totals against the source files after every join. I then wrote a data dictionary that defined each field, its origin and every cleaning decision, so that the next person could rerun the work. Because the survey included addresses and household income, I worked from a pseudonymised copy, stored it only on the lab's approved drive, and removed postcodes before anything left the team. When I found that two analysts had been using different definitions of "persistent absence", I proposed a single written definition and we reran the figures together.

The findings mattered to people who had never seen a regression table. I presented them to a panel of school heads and council transport officers. Rather than show model output, I used a single map-based chart and one sentence per finding: for example, that pupils living more than three kilometres from school with no subsidised fare missed roughly twice as many days as their peers. I gave the heads a one-page summary with three recommendations and gave the transport officers a more detailed version with the assumptions listed. Afterwards, the council asked for the fare-band breakdown to use in a budget paper, which I supplied within a week.

That project was only possible because of regular collaboration. I met the principal investigator and a sociologist every Monday to agree what questions we could answer, and I shared my queries in a version-controlled repository with comments so colleagues could review them. A reviewer's feedback that my first charts were too dense led me to cut them from six panels to two, and the audience response improved noticeably. When a colleague fell ill, I took over her half of the analysis using her documented code and met the submission deadline.

I would bring the same habits to Example Co.: careful SQL, honest checking of the data, plain explanations for managers and a willingness to work openly with the people who rely on the numbers.

I work as an administration officer at Marlowe Street Health Clinic, a six-GP practice, and over the past three years I have become the person colleagues ask when they need numbers pulled from our systems.

My analysis began with a problem. Missed appointments were disrupting clinics, but nobody knew the pattern. I learned SQL to query the read-only reporting copy of our booking database, joining appointments, patient age bands and booking channels, then aggregating by weekday, time slot and lead time. I used Python to tidy the extract and Excel to build pivot tables. The results showed that appointments booked more than three weeks ahead were missed at nearly twice the rate of those booked within a week, at 14 percent against 8 percent across about 22,000 appointments. I have since written a set of monthly queries covering waiting times, referral turnaround and recall lists, and I keep them in a shared folder with comments explaining each step.

I presented the missed appointment findings to the practice manager, the GPs and the reception team. For the GPs I used a single chart and a one-line recommendation. For reception I produced a one-page guide on when to send reminders and which patients to phone. We introduced a text reminder at seven days for long-lead bookings, and over the next four months the missed rate for those bookings fell from 14 to 10 percent. I learned that frontline staff respond best to concrete actions rather than percentages, so I now test drafts on a receptionist before circulating them.

Data quality is a large part of my role. While preparing the analysis, I found that about 6 percent of records had no booking channel and that some appointment types had been entered under three different names. I agreed a clean list of definitions with the practice manager, wrote them up in a data dictionary, and added a mandatory field to the booking form. I also check for duplicate patient records each quarter and have corrected over 300. I only work from pseudonymised extracts, removing names and patient ID numbers before analysis, and I follow the clinic's information governance policy on storage and sharing. Once I noticed a spreadsheet with patient names on a shared drive, I reported it and helped move it to a restricted folder.

I work closely with clinicians, receptionists and the practice manager. Before starting a piece of work I ask what decision it will inform, and I agree a deadline and a definition of success. When a GP questioned my treatment of cancelled appointments, I revised the method and noted the change in the documentation. I also showed two colleagues how to refresh the monthly reports themselves, so the work no longer depends on me alone.

I would welcome the chance to apply these habits to sales, inventory and delivery data at Example Co.

I've spent six years on warehouse floors, the last three as a shift supervisor at a regional distribution centre, and the part of the job I love most is the moment a spreadsheet explains something that has been bugging everyone for weeks.

Our site tracked pick rates, dock-to-stock times and order accuracy, but the numbers lived in separate exports from the warehouse system. I taught myself SQL using a read-only reporting database and began writing queries that joined pick transactions to shift rosters and product locations. When mispicks crept up from 0.9% to 1.6% over a quarter, I aggregated errors by aisle, hour and product family in SQL, then pivoted the results in Excel. The pattern was clear: most errors came from two aisles where similar-looking items sat side by side, and from the last hour of the night shift. We changed slotting and added a short mid-shift check, and mispicks fell to 0.8% within eight weeks.

Explaining this was as important as finding it. I built a one-page weekly dashboard in Power BI for the operations manager, and a simple printed chart with traffic-light colours for the team briefing board. With managers I talked about cost per error and returns; with pickers I talked about which aisles to double-check and why. Attendance at the briefings went up because people could see their own improvements.

Along the way I found that the same pallet could be recorded under two location codes after system migrations, which inflated our stock counts. I wrote a query to flag duplicates, found about 140 affected locations, and worked with the inventory controller to correct them. I also wrote a short data dictionary defining each KPI, its source table and how it was calculated, because three people had been calculating "on-time dispatch" three different ways. I only used employee IDs where needed, and replaced them with anonymous codes in anything shared beyond the management team.

I enjoy working with others to get this right. I sit down with finance and operations colleagues to clarify what question they are really asking before I write any code, I share my queries in a team folder with comments, and I have rewritten dashboards several times after feedback. I've spent the last four years as a warehouse supervisor at a regional distribution centre, and the part of the job I enjoy most is the numbers. Every week I track pick rates, order accuracy and dispatch times for a team of twelve, so moving into a Data Analyst role feels like a natural next step.

On the SQL side, I'm still building my skills, but I've made real progress. Our warehouse management system lets me run basic queries, and a colleague in IT taught me how to join the orders table to the dispatch table. I used that to work out why some late deliveries were clustering on Thursdays. It turned out a late-afternoon shift change was delaying the final pick wave. I also keep a detailed Excel workbook with pivot tables for our weekly KPI review, and I've started learning Power BI in my spare time through online courses.

Explaining numbers to people is something I do every day. In my weekly team huddles I put the key figures on a simple whiteboard chart and talk through what they mean for the shift, and I've learned to skip jargon with the pickers and keep it practical. I also send a short summary to the site manager each Friday with a couple of recommendations. When we changed the pick path layout, the team seemed to understand why it mattered because I showed them the before and after times.

I care about getting the data right. Scanner errors sometimes create duplicate or missing records, so I check the totals against the physical stock counts and flag anything that looks off. I haven't formally documented data definitions, though I'd really like to learn how to do that properly.

I work well with others. I regularly sit down with the inventory team and the transport planners to understand what they need from the figures, and I'm happy to take feedback. The site manager once asked me to simplify my report, and I cut it to one page, which everyone preferred.

I'd love the chance to bring my operational knowledge and my enthusiasm for learning to the Insights team at Example Co.

I am applying for the Data Analyst position because I want to continue growing in analysis work that supports real operational decisions. For two years I have worked as a junior analyst at Brightline Freight, a regional logistics company, in a team of four people.

In my daily work I write SQL queries to take data from our shipment and warehouse tables. I join the tables for orders, drivers and delivery routes, and I make summaries by week and by depot. One project I did was to look at late deliveries in the second half of last year. I found that most of the delays came from only three depots, and that they were mostly on Monday mornings. I also use Excel for pivot tables and Power BI for a weekly dashboard that I maintain. I am still learning more advanced SQL like window functions, but I have used them a few times for ranking depots.

About communication, I present my weekly dashboard to the operations managers in a short meeting. In the beginning my slides had too many numbers, so I changed them to have one chart and one main message for each page. After the late delivery analysis, I wrote a one-page summary for the depot supervisors and recommended moving some driver shifts earlier. I think the managers understood it well, because they asked me for similar summaries for other months.

For data quality, I check for missing delivery times and duplicate order numbers before I make any report. When I found duplicates in our monthly file, I told the person responsible for the system and we corrected the problem. I also know that customer addresses and phone numbers are personal data, so I only use the fields I need and I do not send files with those columns by email.

I like to work with other people and I think this is important in a small team. I ask the managers questions before I start, so I understand what they really need, and I share my queries with my colleague so she can check them. She once suggested a simpler way to calculate delivery time, and I changed my method and noted it in our shared folder. I accept feedback easily and I try to meet deadlines, also when the request changes at the last moment.

I believe my experience with logistics data is a good match for Example Co., which also works with sales, inventory and delivery information. I am careful, I am curious about why numbers change, and I am willing to learn from more experienced colleagues in the Insights team. Thank you for considering my application.

I have spent eight years in retail, the last four as a store manager for a regional homewares chain, and I am now moving into analytics. Over the past two years I have been building the skills formally, and I think my operational background is a useful complement to them.

In my current role I began pulling weekly sales and stock reports from our head office system and found them too limited to answer the questions I was asked by my area manager. I taught myself SQL through an evening course and then used a read-only reporting database to join sales, stock and staffing tables. One piece of work looked at why our store was running out of a handful of fast-moving lines on weekends. By comparing daily sales with delivery dates, I showed that most gaps came from a delivery schedule that did not match demand. The area manager raised it with the distribution team, and the delivery day was moved for several stores. I did the analysis in SQL and Excel, and I have also started using Python for cleaning larger files, though I would describe that as developing rather than established.

Explaining numbers to people is something I do daily. I run a short trading meeting each week with around twenty staff, and I have learned to reduce a week of figures to two or three points they can act on. For the stock analysis I produced a one-page summary with a simple chart for the area manager and a shorter version for my team, focused on which lines to check and when. I try to lead with the recommendation and keep the detail available for anyone who wants it.

On data quality, I have regularly found mismatches between system stock counts and what is on the shelf, and I have learned not to trust a figure before checking where it came from. When I built my queries I kept a short note of the tables used and how I defined a stockout, so a colleague could rerun them. I handle staff rota and payroll information as part of my job and understand that it should be shared only with those who need it. I have not yet worked under a formal data governance framework, and I would welcome the chance to learn one.

I work closely with colleagues across stores, head office and the distribution team. For the stock project I asked the replenishment team what they could and could not change before settling on my question, and I adjusted my approach after they pointed out that some lines were supplied by third parties. I am comfortable taking feedback and sharing unfinished work early.

I would bring practical knowledge of how retail and logistics data relates to what actually happens in stores, along with a steady commitment to improving my technical skills.
